thread.title: Spotify’s Inefficient Market Could Persist for a While

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Spotify’s Inefficient Market Could Persist for a While
text:
By Tiernan Ray Updated April 4, 2018 5:27 p.m. ET It ended up being a down day for Spotify Technology ( SPOT ), though it surged into the close to recoup a lot of lost ground.
Shares ended down only $4.79, or 3%, at $144.22, ending a session that saw the stock trade for as little as $135.51, or down 9% from the first-day close on its debut yesterday.
That $135.51 came pretty close to a “reference price” of $132 that existed before the start of yesterday’s trading on The New York Stock Exchange.
Don’t expect a quick resolution to the ups and downs. This is an inefficient market that could continue for awhile.
Rob Sanderson of MKM Partners , who initiated coverage on the stock last week with a Buy rating, and a $200 price target, acknowledges in a phone call this afternoon that “price discovery,” the process of the market reaching some consensus on what it’s worth, "could be all over the map for a while."
The issue for the moment, Sanderson tells me, is what might be described as a Mexican standoff between buyers and sellers, resulting in a very inefficient market for the shares.
Big buyers, like giant funds, want adequate supply , they want liquidity . But the price at the moment is too low for many insider shareholders who are the suppliers at the moment, given that the company sold no shares in yesterday’s debut.
On the supply side, “I’m told by venture capitalists there were bids in the grey market at $25 billion which they declined,” says Sanderson, referring to proposed transactions before the offering that valued Spotify at $25 billion.
That closing price today of $144.22, multiplied by the 177 million common shares outstanding, equals $25.53 billion. VCs who wouldn’t sell at $25 billion are probably unlikely to sell with the stock now just a little bit higher, reckons Sanderson.
On the demand side, "larger funds that want to build a position have complained they can’t get the two million shares or so they need to build up an adequate-sized position,” says Sanderson.
Those big funds are a source of buying for lots of IPO names, they are buyers you have to have come into the stock to support pricing.
All this complicates the observation made yesterday by John Tinker of Gabelli & Co that big funds want Spotify. Yes they do, but only if they can get adequate supply.
If sellers don’t yet have the price they want, and buyers can’t get the liquidity they want, " the market can be very inefficient ,” says Sanderson.
"It’s just one of the question marks about this unorthodox process,” he says, referring to Spotify coming public without the customary underwriting arrangement.
Still, Sanderson is encouraged by today’s volume of trade. It was just under 11 million shares. That’s on top of about 30 million shares yesterday. He thinks that means supply is going in the right direction , even if it’s still low. “I’m pleased to see that kind of number,” he says of the 40 million-share two-day volume.
A stock such as Facebook ( FB ) has an average daily volume of perhaps $22 million shares, and its in a comparable price bracket, at $155 per share.
Of course, “ I don’t know how much that’s turned over and turned over and turned over ,” he says of the volume, meaning, how much of the trading is new shares entering the market and how much is just the same supply changing hands a lot.
He’s inclined to be philosophical and look past the noise. The current price is a “good opportunity” to "start building your position” in Spotify, he argues. “I’m not concerned about this first month or whatever of trading."
"We will get through all this irregularities and [Spotify stock] will eventually settle into just a bear-bull debate, how are fundamentals tracking, how do you feel about their ability to grow profitably, and to acquire subscribers, and to compete with Apple ( AAPL ), and Amazon.com ( AMZN ), and all those things that make fundamental analysis valuable."
That debate is one he looks forward to. “It is not unlike Netflix ( NFLX ) of five or six years ago,” he says, with lots of controversy about the business.
"That’s a wonderful environment for a fundamental analyst who has a high conviction.” After all, “just being in the consensus is not that satisfying."
